tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

- "Is a custom skill better as a CLAUDE.md rule or maybe a hook?" — led to the design rule at the top of this file.

**Harness changes:** Everything listed above in Harness was created this session.

### 2026-09-24 · S4 details, S6 delete, X4 e2e, README, URL state and toasts

Session: [`70daf4c1`](ai/sessions/2026-09-24-70daf4c1-f90d-4c87-83a3-f50089ed21a8.md) · Stories: S4, S6, X1, X3, X4, P1

**Goal:** Check the web screens (list, detail, create, delete) and fill any gaps, run `/verify`, walk the app with the Playwright MCP, then finish the remaining spec stories.

**What the AI did:**

- Audited first. The detail and delete screens the user believed were "mostly added" did not exist: `routes/property.tsx` was a placeholder and the API had no `property`/`deleteProperty` resolvers (SDL only). There was also no Playwright setup, so `pnpm e2e` ran nothing and `verify` passed without e2e.
- Built S4 and S6 with `/graphql-slice` as vertical slices: repository `findById`/`deleteById`, services with a UUID guard (malformed id → `null` / `PropertyNotFoundError`), union mapping in resolvers, a detail view with a weather snapshot section, and a shadcn AlertDialog for delete.
- Added X4 e2e (happy and `success:false` paths) and a README (X3). `pnpm dev` now runs `prisma migrate deploy` so the app starts in 3 commands.
- Follow-up request: list filters and sort kept in the URL (they survive reload; the detail page returns to the same filtered list), toasts on create and delete (Sonner), and labelled coordinates.
- Browser walk via Playwright MCP against the stub: duplicate create, create, filters (`"  HILLS "`, `85A68`, `Fo%`), sort, detail, delete, not-found, 390px width. The AI deleted only its own test rows and left the user's dev data unchanged.
- 7 commits, one per story or concern. Mixed files were split by rebuilding each commit's tree from a snapshot with a script, and each stage was checked with format, lint, typecheck and tests.

**Corrections & surprises:**

- The two e2e "hangs" were real bugs, not slowness. (1) Vite bound only `::1`, so Playwright's IPv4 readiness check waited forever. (2) Playwright couldn't exit because `pnpm exec` (pnpm 12 native) starts children in a new process group that Playwright's teardown doesn't kill. Fix: `exec node_modules/.bin/...` plus a graceful SIGTERM. Piping through `tail` also hid progress, which made the first run look stuck.
- E2e logs showed two Apollo "cache data may be lost" warnings (`Weather` without an id; `Query.properties` shrinking after delete). Fixed with type policies in `apps/web/src/apollo.ts`.
- The reviewer agent returned DONE (13/13 PASS) plus 6 non-blocking findings, and all were fixed. The most useful one: "no Weatherstack request" tests relied on `onUnhandledRequest`, which a swallowed `fetch` would pass. Tests now assert zero recorded requests, confirmed by temporarily injecting a swallowed call. It also found that services other than create-property could import the Weatherstack client without a lint error.
- shadcn CLI prompted to overwrite `button.tsx`; declined. Its Sonner wrapper imported `next-themes` although the app has no theme provider, so the dependency was removed.
- A web test failed once when run as part of the final `verify`. The AI's first diagnosis (a late async toast) was wrong, and its first fix made the test fail every time. Reading Sonner's source showed the store replays active toasts to a new `<Toaster>`; the fix is `toast.dismiss()` in the test `afterEach`. It was folded into the toasts commit (branch not pushed).
- No shadcn skill was installed although the user asked for one; shadcn docs came through context7 instead.

**Prompts worth noting:**

- "Those were mostly added in the previous session, so confirm if there is anything missing" — the audit found this was not the case, so the session built S4 and S6 instead of polishing them.

(2) Playwright couldn't exit because `pnpm exec` (pnpm 12 native) starts children in a new process group that Playwright's teardown doesn't kill. Fix: `exec node_modules/.bin/...` plus a graceful SIGTERM. Piping through `tail` also hid progress, which made the first run look stuck.
- E2e logs showed two Apollo "cache data may be lost" warnings (`Weather` without an id; `Query.properties` shrinking after delete). Fixed with type policies in `apps/web/src/apollo.ts`.
- The reviewer agent returned DONE (13/13 PASS) plus 6 non-blocking findings, and all were fixed. The most useful one: "no Weatherstack request" tests relied on `onUnhandledRequest`, which a swallowed `fetch` would pass. Tests now assert zero recorded requests, confirmed by temporarily injecting a swallowed call. It also found that services other than create-property could import the Weatherstack client without a lint error.
- shadcn CLI prompted to overwrite `button.tsx`; declined. Its Sonner wrapper imported `next-themes` although the app has no theme provider, so the dependency was removed.
- A web test failed once when run as part of the final `verify`. The AI's first diagnosis (a late async toast) was wrong, and its first fix made the test fail every time. Reading Sonner's source showed the store replays active toasts to a new `<Toaster>`; the fix is `toast.dismiss()` in the test `afterEach`. It was folded into the toasts commit (branch not pushed).
- No shadcn skill was installed although the user asked for one; shadcn docs came through context7 instead.

**Prompts worth noting:**

- "Those were mostly added in the previous session, so confirm if there is anything missing" — the audit found this was not the case, so the session built S4 and S6 instead of polishing them.

---CI
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:

concurrency:
  group: ci-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

jobs:
  verify:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 20
    services:
      postgres-test:
        image: postgres:17-alpine
        env:
          POSTGRES_USER: covertree
          POSTGRES_PASSWORD: [REDACTED]
          POSTGRES_DB: covertree_test
        ports: ['5433:5432']
        options: >-
          --health-cmd "pg_isready -U covertree -d covertree_test"
          --health-interval 2s --health-timeout 3s --health-retries 15
    env:
      # Same values as .env.example; CI never has a real Weatherstack key (tests use MSW / a stub).
      TEST_DATABASE_URL: postgresql://[REDACTED]@localhost:5433/covertree_test
      DATABASE_URL: postgresql://[REDACTED]@localhost:5433/covertree_test
      WEATHERSTACK_BASE_URL: http://localhost:4999
      WEATHERSTACK_ACCESS_KEY: [REDACTED]
      VITE_GRAPHQL_URL: http://localhost:4000/graphql
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: pnpm/action-setup@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version-file: .nvmrc
          cache: pnpm
      - run: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
      - name: Install Playwright browser
        if: hashFiles('apps/web/playwright.config.ts') != ''
        run: pnpm --filter web exec playwright install --with-deps chromium
      - run: pnpm run verify
      - name: Upload Playwright report
        if: failure() && hashFiles('apps/web/playwright-report/**') != ''
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: playwright-report
          path: apps/web/playwright-report
---README
# Covertree properties

GraphQL API (`apps/api`, GraphQL Yoga + Prisma + Postgres) and React app (`apps/web`, Vite +
Apollo Client + shadcn/ui) for US property records. Creating a property records the current
Weatherstack weather and the location's latitude/longitude with it.

- Contract and acceptance criteria: [docs/SPEC.md](docs/SPEC.md)
- Design decisions: [docs/adr/](docs/adr/)
- How the AI tooling was used: [AI_WORKFLOW.md](AI_WORKFLOW.md)

## Prerequisites

- Node.js 22+
- pnpm 12 (`corepack enable` picks up the version pinned in `package.json`)
- Docker (Docker Desktop or OrbStack) for Postgres
- A [Weatherstack](https://weatherstack.com) access key (the free tier works) to create properties
  against the real service. Tests never use it.

## Setup

```sh
cp .env.example .env   # then set WEATHERSTACK_ACCESS_KEY
```

The defaults in `.env.example` match `docker-compose.yml`. The free Weatherstack tier is HTTP-only,
so keep `WEATHERSTACK_BASE_URL=http://api.weatherstack.com`.

## Run

```sh
docker compose up -d --wait   # Postgres: dev on :5432, test on :5433
pnpm install                  # also generates Prisma client and GraphQL types
pnpm dev                      # applies migrations; API http://localhost:4000/graphql, web http://localhost:5173
```

To run the app without spending Weatherstack quota, start the local stub and point the API at it:

```sh
node apps/web/e2e/weatherstack-stub.mjs            # :4999, always returns Fountain Hills weather
WEATHERSTACK_BASE_URL=http://localhost:4999 pnpm dev
```

## Test

```sh
pnpm test          # unit + integration (API against postgres-test, web with MSW)
pnpm test:unit     # fast subset, no database
pnpm e2e           # Playwright: create → list → filter → detail → delete, plus the weather-failure path
pnpm verify        # everything CI runs: format, lint, typecheck, tests, build, e2e
```

The first time you run e2e, install its browser with
`pnpm --filter web exec playwright install chromium`.

No test calls the real Weatherstack. Unit and integration tests use MSW with unhandled requests
failing the test. E2E starts its own stack on separate ports (stub :4999, API :4100, web :5174)
against the test database, so a running `pnpm dev` is never touched.

## Layout

```
apps/api   schema.graphql (the contract) → resolvers → services → repositories (Prisma)
apps/web   routes + features/properties, typed by codegen from the API schema (src/gql)
docs       SPEC and ADRs
```

  },
  "scripts": {
    "dev": "pnpm -r --parallel --if-present dev",

entries.name: mcp__context7__query-docs
entries.description:
Retrieves and queries up-to-date documentation and code examples from Context7 for any programming library or framework.

You must call 'Resolve Context7 Library ID' tool first to obtain the exact Context7-compatible library ID required to use this tool, UNLESS the user explicitly provides a library ID in the format '/org/project' or '/org/project/version' in their query.

Do not call this tool more than 3 times per question.

libraryId.description: Exact Context7-compatible library ID (e.g., '/mongodb/docs', '/vercel/next.js', '/supabase/supabase', '/vercel/next.js/v14.3.0-canary.87') retrieved from 'resolve-library-id' or directly from user query in the format '/org/project' or '/org/project/version'.

query.description: What to look up in the library's documentation, scoped to a single concept. Be specific and include relevant details, but keep each query to one topic — if the user's question spans multiple distinct concepts, make a separate call per concept instead of combining them, unless the question is about how the concepts interact. Good: 'How to set up authentication with JWT in Express.js' or 'React useEffect cleanup function examples'. Bad (too vague): 'auth' or 'hooks'. Bad (too broad): 'routing and auth and caching in Next.js'. The query is sent to the Context7 API for processing. Do not include any sensitive or confidential information such as API keys, passwords, credentials, personal data, or proprietary code in your query.

entries.name: mcp__context7__resolve-library-id
entries.description:
Resolves a package/product name to a Context7-compatible library ID and returns matching libraries.

You MUST call this function before 'Query Documentation' tool to obtain a valid Context7-compatible library ID UNLESS the user explicitly provides a library ID in the format '/org/project' or '/org/project/version' in their query.

Each result includes:
- Library ID: Context7-compatible identifier (format: /org/project)
- Name: Library or package name
- Description: Short summary
- Code Snippets: Number of available code examples
- Source Reputation: Authority indicator (High, Medium, Low, or Unknown)
- Benchmark Score: Quality indicator (100 is the highest score)
- Versions: List of versions if available. Use one of those versions if the user provides a version in their query. The format of the version is /org/project/version.

For best results, select libraries based on name match, source reputation, snippet coverage, benchmark score, and relevance to your use case.

Selection Process:
1. Analyze the query to understand what library/package the user is looking for
2. Return the most relevant match based on:
- Name similarity to the query (exact matches prioritized)
- Description relevance to the query's intent
- Documentation coverage (prioritize libraries with higher Code Snippet counts)
- Source reputation (consider libraries with High or Medium reputation more authoritative)
- Benchmark Score: Quality indicator (100 is the highest score)

Response Format:
- Return the selected library ID in a clearly marked section
- Provide a brief explanation for why this library was chosen
- If multiple good matches exist, acknowledge this but proceed with the most relevant one
- If no good matches exist, clearly state this and suggest query refinements

For ambiguous queries, request clarification before proceeding with a best-guess match.

IMPORTANT: Do not call this tool more than 3 times per question. If you cannot find what you need after 3 calls, use the best result you have.

query.description: What to look up in the library's documentation. This is used to rank library results by relevance to what the user is trying to accomplish. The query is sent to the Context7 API for processing. Do not include any sensitive or confidential information such as API keys, passwords, credentials, personal data, or proprietary code in your query.

libraryName.description: Library name to search for and retrieve a Context7-compatible library ID. Use the official library name with proper punctuation — e.g., 'Next.js' instead of 'nextjs', 'Customer.io' instead of 'customerio', 'Three.js' instead of 'threejs'.

### Run prisma migrate diff with --from-config-datasource in Prisma v7

Source: https://www.prisma.io/docs/ai/prompts/prisma-7

Execute schema comparison in Prisma v7 using the configuration datasource flag instead of URL flags.

```bash
prisma migrate diff \
  --from-config-datasource \
  --to-schema schema.prisma \
  --script
```

--------------------------------

### Configure shadowDatabaseUrl in prisma.config.ts

Source: https://www.prisma.io/docs/orm/v7/prisma-migrate/understanding-prisma-migrate/shadow-database

Sets the `shadowDatabaseUrl` in `prisma.config.ts` to manually designate a dedicated shadow database for `migrate dev`. Never use identical values for `url` and `shadowDatabaseUrl` as it can delete all database data.

```typescript
import "dotenv/config";
import { defineConfig, env } from "prisma/config";

export default defineConfig({
  schema: "prisma/schema.prisma",
  migrations: {
    path: "prisma/migrations",
  },
  datasource: {
    url: env("DATABASE_URL"),
    shadowDatabaseUrl: env("SHADOW_DATABASE_URL"), // [!code highlight]
  },
});
```

--------------------------------

### Compare a Prisma schema to the configured database

Source: https://www.prisma.io/docs/orm/v7/reference/prisma-cli-reference

Compares a Prisma schema against the database datasource defined in prisma.config.ts and outputs the diff as a SQL script.

```bash
prisma migrate diff \
  --from-schema=schema.prisma \
  --to-config-datasource \
  --script
```

---
name: verify
description: Run the full quality gate for the property app (Postgres up, `pnpm verify` = format, lint, typecheck, all tests, build, e2e) and then smoke-test the running UI in a real browser via the Playwright MCP, reporting each failure with its likely cause. Use this before any commit or PR, after finishing a story, when the user asks "does everything pass?", "is it green?", "check it works", "run the checks", or wants to confirm the app actually runs, even if they don't say "verify".
---

# Verify

The Stop hook already typechecks and unit-tests after every turn. This skill is the **full** gate:
the checks that need Docker, a build, or a browser, plus judgment about what a failure means.
`pnpm verify` is the single source of truth, and CI runs the same script, so don't reimplement its
steps here.

## 1. Database

Run `docker compose ps`. If Docker itself isn't running (connection refused), tell the user to
start OrbStack/Docker Desktop and stop there. Otherwise run `docker compose up -d --wait` so both
`postgres` and `postgres-test` are healthy before tests start. If the api exists, apply migrations
to the dev DB with `pnpm --filter api exec prisma migrate deploy`.

## 2. The gate

Run `pnpm run verify`. It stops at the first failing stage, in this order: format:check → lint →
typecheck → test → build → e2e. For the failing stage:

- **format:check:** run `pnpm run format`; nothing to diagnose.
- **lint:** a `no-restricted-imports` error means a layering violation (see CLAUDE.md). Move the
  code to the right layer; don't disable the rule.
- **typecheck:** first check whether codegen is stale (`pnpm run codegen`, then retry). Stale
  generated types are the most common cause after a schema edit.
- **test:** an MSW `onUnhandledRequest` error means code is calling a URL with no handler, often

    for a,b in sc.items():

# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
# One Dockerfile for the monorepo; docker-compose.yml builds the `api` and `web` targets.

FROM node:22-slim AS base
# openssl: Prisma's schema engine (`migrate deploy`) links against it.
RUN apt-get update \
  && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends openssl ca-certificates \
  && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/* \
  && npm install -g pnpm@12.6.0
WORKDIR /app

# Dependencies are fetched from the lockfile alone, so this layer survives source edits.
FROM base AS deps
COPY pnpm-lock.yaml pnpm-workspace.yaml ./
RUN pnpm fetch
COPY . .
# postinstall runs `prisma generate` (the Prisma client is not committed).
RUN pnpm install --offline --frozen-lockfile

FROM deps AS api
RUN pnpm --filter api build
WORKDIR /app/apps/api
ENV NODE_ENV=production
EXPOSE 4000
# Dev dependencies stay installed: the Prisma CLI applies migrations on start.
CMD ["sh", "-c", "node_modules/.bin/prisma migrate deploy && exec node dist/server.js"]

FROM deps AS web-build
# Inlined at build time; the browser calls the API directly.
ARG VITE_GRAPHQL_URL=http://localhost:4000/graphql
ENV VITE_GRAPHQL_URL=$VITE_GRAPHQL_URL
RUN pnpm --filter web build

FROM nginx:1.29-alpine AS web
COPY apps/web/nginx.conf /etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf
COPY --from=web-build /app/apps/web/dist /usr/share/nginx/html

name: Setup

runs:

  steps:
    - uses: pnpm/action-setup@v4

name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:

concurrency:
  group: ci-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

# Same values as .env.example; CI never has a real Weatherstack key (tests use MSW / a stub).
env:
  TEST_DATABASE_URL: postgresql://[REDACTED]@localhost:5433/covertree_test
  DATABASE_URL: postgresql://[REDACTED]@localhost:5433/covertree_test
  WEATHERSTACK_BASE_URL: http://localhost:4999
  WEATHERSTACK_ACCESS_KEY: [REDACTED]
  VITE_GRAPHQL_URL: http://localhost:4000/graphql

jobs:
  lint:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 10
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: ./.github/actions/setup
      - run: pnpm run format:check
      - run: pnpm run lint

  typecheck:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 10
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: ./.github/actions/setup
      - run: pnpm run typecheck

  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 15
    services:
      postgres-test: &postgres-test
        image: postgres:17-alpine
        env:
          POSTGRES_USER: covertree
          POSTGRES_PASSWORD: [REDACTED]
          POSTGRES_DB: covertree_test
        ports: ['5433:5432']
        options: >-
          --health-cmd "pg_isready -U covertree -d covertree_test"
          --health-interval 2s --health-timeout 3s --health-retries 15
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: ./.github/actions/setup
      - run: pnpm run test

  codegen:
    name: codegen drift
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 10
    services:
      postgres-test: *postgres-test
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: ./.github/actions/setup
      - name: GraphQL types match schema.graphql and the web documents
        run: pnpm run codegen:check
      - name: Prisma migrations match schema.prisma
        run: pnpm --filter api run db:drift

  e2e:
    name: build + e2e
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 20
    services:
      postgres-test: *postgres-test
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: ./.github/actions/setup
      - run: pnpm run build
      - run: pnpm --filter web exec playwright install --with-deps chromium
      - run: pnpm run e2e
      - name: Upload Playwright report
        if: failure() && hashFiles('apps/web/playwright-report/**') != ''
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: playwright-report
          path: apps/web/playwright-report

  docker:
    name: docker images
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 15
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: docker compose build
EOF

# Covertree properties

GraphQL API (`apps/api`, GraphQL Yoga + Prisma + Postgres) and React app (`apps/web`, Vite +
Apollo Client + shadcn/ui) for US property records. Creating a property records the current
Weatherstack weather and the location's latitude/longitude with it.

- Contract and acceptance criteria: [docs/SPEC.md](docs/SPEC.md)
- Design decisions: [docs/adr/](docs/adr/)
- How the AI tooling was used: [AI_WORKFLOW.md](AI_WORKFLOW.md)

## Quick start (one command)

Needs Docker only. Put your Weatherstack key in `.env`, then start Postgres, the API and the web
app:

```sh
cp .env.example .env   # set WEATHERSTACK_ACCESS_KEY
docker compose up --build
```

Open http://localhost:5173 (API: http://localhost:4000/graphql). The API applies migrations on
start.

No key, or want to save quota? Use the local Weatherstack stub. It always returns the same
Fountain Hills, AZ weather:

```sh
docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.stub.yml up --build
```

## Environment variables

Copy `.env.example` to `.env` at the repo root. Both apps read it; `.env` is never committed.

| Variable                  | Used by   | Default in `.env.example`                                        | Notes                                                                              |
| ------------------------- | --------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `WEATHERSTACK_ACCESS_KEY` | API       | `your-access-key`                                                | **Required.** Your Weatherstack key.                                               |
| `WEATHERSTACK_BASE_URL`   | API       | `http://api.weatherstack.com`                                    | Keep `http://` on the free plan (see below). `http://localhost:4999` for the stub. |
| `DATABASE_URL`            | API       | `postgresql://[REDACTED]@localhost:5432/covertree`      | Dev database (`postgres` service).                                                 |
| `TEST_DATABASE_URL`       | API tests | `postgresql://[REDACTED]@localhost:5433/covertree_test` | Integration tests and e2e (`postgres-test` service, tmpfs).                        |
| `PORT`                    | API       | `4000`                                                           |                                                                                    |
| `VITE_GRAPHQL_URL`        | web       | `http://localhost:4000/graphql`                                  | Inlined at build time.                                                             |

The API checks its variables on start and exits naming any that are missing or invalid.
`docker compose up` only takes `WEATHERSTACK_ACCESS_KEY` from `.env`. It sets the rest itself, so
the containers reach each other by service name.

## Weatherstack plan

The app works on Weatherstack's **free plan**, with two limits:

- **HTTP only.** The free plan rejects `https://` requests (error 105), so the base URL is
  `http://api.weatherstack.com`. The key travels in the query string over plain HTTP, so use a
  paid plan and `https://` for anything beyond local use.
- **About 100 calls a month.** Only `createProperty` calls Weatherstack, once per property.
  Invalid input and duplicates are rejected before the call, so they don't use quota. Listing,
  details and delete read from Postgres. When the quota runs out, Weatherstack answers HTTP 200
  with `success: false`. The API reports that as `WeatherUnavailableError { reason: UPSTREAM_ERROR }`
  and saves nothing ([ADR 0004](docs/adr/0004-weather-failure-policy.md)).

Tests never call Weatherstack, so they cost no quota. For manual testing, use the stub.

## Architecture

```
 Browser ── React app (apps/web) ── Apollo Client, types generated from the schema (src/gql)
                  │
                  │ GraphQL over HTTP
                  ▼
 GraphQL Yoga (apps/api) ── schema.graphql is the contract; codegen → resolver types
   resolvers      map GraphQL ⇄ service calls; domain results → union types (…Success | …Error)
      │
   services       validation (Zod for what SDL can't express), business rules; no GraphQL imports
      │    └──────────────▶ Weatherstack client  (create-property service only; injected via context,
      │                      response parsed with Zod)                ──▶ api.weatherstack.com
   repositories   the only Prisma users
      │
   PostgreSQL 17  (docker compose: dev :5432, test :5433)
```

ESLint `no-restricted-imports` enforces the layering. The generated GraphQL types are committed,
and CI fails if they are out of date. The ADRs record the reasons: Yoga over Apollo Server, Prisma
over Drizzle, and failing creation when the weather lookup fails.

## Develop without Docker for the apps

Node.js 22+ and pnpm 12 (`corepack enable`). Postgres still runs in Docker:

```sh
docker compose up -d --wait postgres postgres-test   # databases only
pnpm install                                         # also generates the Prisma client
pnpm dev                                             # applies migrations; API :4000, web :5173 (hot reload)
```

To use the stub instead of real Weatherstack:

```sh
node apps/web/e2e/weatherstack-stub.mjs              # :4999
WEATHERSTACK_BASE_URL=http://localhost:4999 pnpm dev
```

After editing `apps/api/src/schema.graphql` or a query in `apps/web`, run `pnpm codegen` and
commit the regenerated types. For a schema change to the database, run
`pnpm --filter api exec prisma migrate dev --name <change>`.

## Tests

Start the test database first with `docker compose up -d --wait postgres-test`.

```sh
pnpm test            # unit + integration (API against postgres-test, web with MSW)
pnpm test:unit       # fast subset, no database
pnpm e2e             # Playwright: create → list → filter → detail → delete, plus the weather-failure path
pnpm verify          # format, lint, typecheck, tests, build, e2e
pnpm codegen:check   # generated GraphQL types match the schema and documents
```

The first time you run e2e, install its browser with
`pnpm --filter web exec playwright install chromium`.

No test calls the real Weatherstack. Unit and integration tests use MSW, and any unhandled request
fails the test. E2E starts its own stack on separate ports (stub :4999, API :4100, web :5174)
against the test database, so a running `pnpm dev` or `docker compose` stack is never touched.

CI ([`.github/workflows/ci.yml`](.github/workflows/ci.yml)) runs these as separate jobs: lint
(Prettier + ESLint), typecheck, test, **codegen drift** (GraphQL types plus a check that Prisma
migrations match `schema.prisma`), build + e2e, and a Docker image build.

# Covertree properties

GraphQL API (`apps/api`, GraphQL Yoga + Prisma + Postgres) and React app (`apps/web`, Vite +
Apollo Client + shadcn/ui) for US property records. Creating a property records the current
Weatherstack weather and the location's latitude/longitude with it.

- Contract and acceptance criteria: [docs/SPEC.md](docs/SPEC.md)
- Design decisions: [docs/adr/](docs/adr/)
- How the AI tooling was used: [AI_WORKFLOW.md](AI_WORKFLOW.md)

## Prerequisites

- Node.js 22+
- pnpm 12 (`corepack enable` picks up the version pinned in `package.json`)
- Docker (Docker Desktop or OrbStack) for Postgres
- A [Weatherstack](https://weatherstack.com) access key (the free tier works) to create properties
  against the real service. Tests never use it.

## Setup

```sh
cp .env.example .env   # then set WEATHERSTACK_ACCESS_KEY
```

The defaults in `.env.example` match `docker-compose.yml`. The free Weatherstack tier is HTTP-only,
so keep `WEATHERSTACK_BASE_URL=http://api.weatherstack.com`.

## Run

```sh
docker compose up -d --wait   # Postgres: dev on :5432, test on :5433
pnpm install                  # also generates Prisma client and GraphQL types
pnpm dev                      # applies migrations; API http://localhost:4000/graphql, web http://localhost:5173
```

To run the app without spending Weatherstack quota, start the local stub and point the API at it:

```sh
node apps/web/e2e/weatherstack-stub.mjs            # :4999, always returns Fountain Hills weather
WEATHERSTACK_BASE_URL=http://localhost:4999 pnpm dev
```

## Test

```sh
pnpm test          # unit + integration (API against postgres-test, web with MSW)
pnpm test:unit     # fast subset, no database
pnpm e2e           # Playwright: create → list → filter → detail → delete, plus the weather-failure path
pnpm verify        # everything CI runs: format, lint, typecheck, tests, build, e2e
```

The first time you run e2e, install its browser with
`pnpm --filter web exec playwright install chromium`.

No test calls the real Weatherstack. Unit and integration tests use MSW with unhandled requests
failing the test. E2E starts its own stack on separate ports (stub :4999, API :4100, web :5174)
against the test database, so a running `pnpm dev` is never touched.

## Layout

```
apps/api   schema.graphql (the contract) → resolvers → services → repositories (Prisma)
apps/web   routes + features/properties, typed by codegen from the API schema (src/gql)
docs       SPEC and ADRs
```

**Docker Compose**
- **One command:** `docker compose up --build` now starts Postgres, the API (:4000) and the web app (:5173). A single root `Dockerfile` builds both images, and the web app is served by nginx.
- **Missing key:** Compose reads `WEATHERSTACK_ACCESS_KEY` from `.env`. If it's missing, the API stops at startup and names the variable.
- **Stub mode:** `docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose.stub.yml up --build` runs against the local Weatherstack stub, so no key or quota is needed.
- **Smoke test:** I ran the full stack in stub mode as a separate Compose project on other ports, because your `pnpm dev` API is on :4000. Create and list worked through the API, a deep link to a detail page loaded in the browser with no console errors, and CORS worked. I tore that project down afterwards. Your dev database wasn't touched.
- **Database-only start:** now `docker compose up -d --wait postgres postgres-test`. I updated CLAUDE.md, the `/verify` skill and the scaffold notes, because a plain `up` would now also try to bind :4000/:5173.

**GitHub Actions** (`.github/workflows/ci.yml`, sharing one setup step)
- **Jobs:** lint (Prettier + ESLint), typecheck, test, and codegen drift.
- **Codegen drift:** the generated GraphQL types are now committed and currently staged. `pnpm codegen:check` regenerates them and fails on any difference. A second step, `pnpm --filter api db:drift`, fails when `schema.prisma` has a change with no migration. I tested both: a stale query and an unmigrated column each made them fail. The Prisma client itself stays gitignored.
- **Extra jobs:** build + e2e, so the split doesn't drop the coverage the old single job had, and a Docker image build so the Dockerfile can't break unnoticed.
- **Unverified on GitHub:** the workflow uses YAML anchors to share the Postgres service definition. GitHub Actions supports them, but we'll only know it works once it runs on GitHub.

**README:** it now has all six sections: one-command start, an env var table, the Weatherstack plan note, an architecture diagram, how to run tests, and the link to `AI_WORKFLOW.md`. The plan note covers the HTTP-only free plan with its key-over-HTTP caveat, the roughly 100 calls a month, which operations use quota, and what running out looks like. The quota figure comes from ADR 0001/0004.

Nothing is committed yet, and neither `pnpm test` nor `pnpm e2e` has run since these changes. When we get there I'd split it into three commits: the list skeleton, the Docker files, then CI + codegen drift + README. Next up is the reviewer pass over S1–S7.

# Verify

The Stop hook already typechecks and unit-tests after every turn. This skill is the **full** gate:
the checks that need Docker, a build, or a browser, plus judgment about what a failure means.
`pnpm verify` is the single source of truth, and CI runs the same stages as separate jobs (plus a
codegen drift check and a Docker build), so don't reimplement its steps here.

## 1. Database

Run `docker compose ps`. If Docker itself isn't running (connection refused), tell the user to
start OrbStack/Docker Desktop and stop there. Otherwise run `docker compose up -d --wait postgres postgres-test` (naming the services;
the default set also starts the api/web containers on :4000/:5173) so both
`postgres` and `postgres-test` are healthy before tests start. If the api exists, apply migrations
to the dev DB with `pnpm --filter api exec prisma migrate deploy`.

## 2. The gate

Run `pnpm run verify`. It stops at the first failing stage, in this order: format:check → lint →
typecheck → test → build → e2e. For the failing stage:

- **format:check:** run `pnpm run format`; nothing to diagnose.
- **lint:** a `no-restricted-imports` error means a layering violation (see CLAUDE.md). Move the
  code to the right layer; don't disable the rule.
- **typecheck:** first check whether codegen is stale (`pnpm run codegen`, then retry). Stale
  generated types are the most common cause after a schema edit.
- **test:** an MSW `onUnhandledRequest` error means code is calling a URL with no handler, often
  the real Weatherstack. That's a bug in the code or a missing handler, never a reason to relax the
  setting.
- **e2e:** check that the Weatherstack stub and api `webServer`s started (port conflicts, missing
  migrations on the test DB).

Fix what's clearly in scope for the current work and re-run. Otherwise report it.

## 3. UI smoke (only if `apps/web` exists)

A green e2e run proves the scripted path. This step is a human-style look at the running app, to
catch what assertions miss: broken layout, console errors, confusing states.

1. Start the stack in the background against the **Weatherstack stub**, not the real API, so no
   quota is spent. Use the e2e stub
   (`node apps/web/e2e/weatherstack-stub.mjs`) and start the api with
   `WEATHERSTACK_BASE_URL=http://localhost:4999`, then `pnpm dev`. Use the real API only if the user
   explicitly asks.
2. Using the Playwright MCP tools, walk the SPEC X4 path with the PDF example (15528 E Golden Eagle
   Blvd, Fountain Hills, AZ 85268): create → it appears in the list with weather → filter by
   city/zip/state → open detail (lat/long, weather) → delete → it's gone.
3. Take a screenshot of the list and detail pages, and read the browser console for errors.
4. Stop the background processes you started.

## 4. Report

Use exactly this shape:

```
## Verify: PASS | FAIL
| Stage | Result | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| database | ✅ | postgres, postgres-test healthy |
| format · lint · typecheck | ✅ | |
| test | ❌ | 2 failing: S5.5 timeout case (apps/api/test/…:88) |
| build · e2e | ⏭ skipped | gate stopped at test |
| UI smoke | ⏭ / ✅ / ❌ | console errors, screenshots |

**Likely cause:** <one or two sentences per failure, pointing at file:line>
**Next step:** <the concrete fix, or what you need from the user>
```

Only report PASS when every stage ran and passed. A skipped stage is not a pass.

content.text:
Review target: `Scope: the whole repo, i.e. main...HEAD (main has no app code). REPORT ONLY — do not edit any files or apply fixes; list each proposed cleanup with file:line, what to change, and why. The user will choose which to apply. Skip generated files (apps/api/src/__generated__, apps/web/src/gql) and ai/sessions.`

`/simplify → 4 cleanup agents in parallel → apply the fixes`

You are improving the quality of the changed code, not hunting for bugs. Review
it for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude issues, then fix what you
find. Do not look for correctness bugs — that is what `/code-review` is for.

## Phase 0 — Gather the diff

Run `git diff @{upstream}...HEAD` (or `git diff main...HEAD` / `git diff HEAD~1`
if there's no upstream) to get the unified diff under review. If there are
uncommitted changes, or the range diff is empty, also run `git diff HEAD` and
include the working-tree changes in scope — the review often runs before the
commit. If a PR number, branch name, or file path was passed as an argument,
review that target instead. Treat this diff as the review scope.

## Phase 1 — Review (4 cleanup agents in parallel)

Launch **4 independent review agents** via the Agent tool, all in a
single message so they run concurrently. Pass each agent the diff and one of
the four angles below. Each returns its findings with `file`, `line`, a
one-line `summary`, and the concrete cost (what is duplicated, wasted, or
harder to maintain).

### Reuse

Flag new code that re-implements something the codebase
already has — Grep shared/utility modules and files adjacent to the change,
and name the existing helper to call instead.

### Simplification

Flag unnecessary complexity the diff adds: redundant or derivable state,
copy-paste with slight variation, deep nesting, dead code left behind. Name
the simpler form that does the same job.

### Efficiency

Flag wasted work the diff introduces: redundant computation or repeated I/O,
independent operations run sequentially, blocking work added to startup or
hot paths. Also flag long-lived objects built from closures or captured
environments — they keep the entire enclosing scope alive for the object's
lifetime (a memory leak when that scope holds large values); prefer a
class/struct that copies only the fields it needs. Name the cheaper
alternative.

### Altitude

Check that each change fixes the root cause at the right depth rather than
patching a symptom with a fragile bandaid. Special cases layered on shared
infrastructure are a sign the fix isn't deep enough — prefer the simpler, more
general change to the underlying mechanism over adding special cases, and name
that change.

## Phase 2 — Apply the fixes

Wait for all four agents to complete, dedup findings that point at the same
line or mechanism, and fix each remaining one directly. Skip any finding whose
fix would change intended behavior, require changes well outside the reviewed
diff, or that you judge to be a false positive — note the skip rather than
arguing with it. Finish with a brief summary of what was fixed and what was
skipped (or confirm the code was already clean).

- list filtering (wildcard escaping, blank and bad zip handling);
- id checks for get and delete, and the resolver mappings;
- Apollo cache updates after create and delete, and the URL-driven list state;
- the Docker, compose and env loading setup.</result>

  ## Altitude review: chore/ai-harness vs main (read-only)
  
  These are fixes that sit at the wrong layer, ordered by value. Each one names the underlying change that would remove the bandaid.
  
  1. **apps/web/src/features/properties/property-list.tsx:41-43**: `fetchPolicy: 'cache-and-network'` makes up for the create mutation never touching the cache. The comment says so: the list is unmounted during create, so a named refetch would miss it.
     - **Root change:** in `create-property-form.tsx`, give `useMutation(CreatePropertyMutation)` an `update(cache) { cache.evict({ fieldName: 'properties' }); cache.gc(); }` on success. That mirrors the evict that `delete-property-button.tsx:36` already does. Then drop the per-query policy.
     - **Cost:** every visit to the list (back link, after delete, back/forward) does a network round-trip, even though the cache is valid. Cache invalidation is also split two ways: delete evicts, create relies on the list always refetching.
  
  2. **apps/api/test/create-property.int.test.ts:16-31**: the test rebuilds the whole service graph by hand (all four services, repository, Weatherstack client). It does this only to set `timeoutMs: 100` and a silent `logger`, because `createServices` (apps/api/src/container.ts:17) takes no options.
     - **Root change:** let `createServices(env, prisma, { weatherstackTimeoutMs?, logger? })` accept overrides, or accept an optional prebuilt `weatherstack` client.
     - **Cost:** this is a second copy of the container. A new service or dependency has to be added in two places, and this test no longer exercises the real wiring.
  
  3. **apps/api/test/*.int.test.ts** (for example delete-property.int.test.ts:11,42-43, property-details.int.test.ts:11,42-43, db.int.test.ts:5-6): every integration file repeats `beforeEach(resetTables)`, `afterAll(() => testPrisma.$disconnect())` and `createApp({ services: createServices(readEnv(), testPrisma) })`. `database.ts:9` even documents "call in `beforeEach`" as a per-file duty.
     - **Root change:** give the `integration` project in apps/api/vitest.config.ts its own `setupFiles` entry that registers the reset and disconnect hooks, plus a `test/app.ts` helper that exports the wired app.
     - **Cost:** a new test file that forgets `resetTables` sees rows from earlier files and fails depending on test order.
  
  4. **apps/web/playwright.config.ts:13-20, 45 and apps/web/e2e/properties.spec.ts:3-4, 80-93**: e2e shares `covertree_test` with the integration tests.
     - That forces several workarounds:
       - a comment "never run the two at once" (ordering enforced only by `pnpm verify`)
       - `Date.now()` streets so leftover rows don't collide
       - the failure-path test snapshotting the existing rows and comparing before/after, instead of asserting on a known state
     - **Root change:** give e2e its own database (for example `covertree_e2e` on the same postgres-test container) and truncate it in a Playwright `globalSetup`.
     - **Cost:** hidden ordering coupling between two test suites, and e2e assertions weakened to fit whatever data is already there.
  
  5. **apps/web/playwright.config.ts:15-20, apps/api/test/global-setup.int.ts:7, apps/api/test/test-database-url.ts:2-4**: the test database URL default and the `:5433/` safety guard are copied in three places. `prisma migrate deploy` is also run separately by the Playwright api webServer command (line 45) and by global-setup.
     - **Root change:** have test-database-url.ts export the URL and an `assertTestDatabase(url)` function, and import both from the Playwright config.
     - **Cost:** changing the port or database name means editing three guards, and one of them can silently fall out of sync.
  
  6. **apps/api/src/services/delete-property.service.ts:16-18, get-property.service.ts:12, repositories/property.repository.ts:42,47**: the repository's contract says "`id` must already be a well-formed UUID". That pushes a Postgres detail up into every service: each calls `isPropertyId`, and delete re-derives how Postgres stores the id with `id.toLowerCase()`, with a comment explaining it.
     - **Root change:** the repository owns id handling. `findById` / `deleteById` return null/false for a malformed id, and `deleteById` returns the deleted row's id (for example `delete` with a P2025 catch, or `deleteMany` plus a select) instead of a boolean.
     - **Cost:** every future by-id service has to remember the guard, and the service guesses the database's canonical form.
  
  7. **apps/api/src/resolvers/property.resolvers.ts:69, 76**: `property.weatherData as unknown as ResolversTypes['Weather']` casts untyped Prisma JSON at the GraphQL layer. `weatherDescriptions.map(trim)` cleans upstream data on every read.
     - **Root change:** the repository's record mapper should return a typed `weatherData`, parsed with `WeatherstackCurrent` in apps/api/src/weatherstack/schema.ts. The trim belongs in that schema (`z.array(z.string().trim())`), so the data is normalized once, when it is stored.
     - **Cost:** the resolver trusts stored JSON blindly, so a malformed row fails in serialization rather than at a typed boundary. Data normalization is spread across ingestion and presentation.
  
  8. **apps/api/src/env.ts:15-16**: `if (source === process.env) loadRootEnv()` checks object identity inside a shared function to decide whether to read `.env`, so tests "stay pure".
     - **Root change:** call `loadRootEnv()` once at the entrypoints (server.ts, weatherstack-probe.ts) and keep `readEnv` a pure parser.
     - **Cost:** hidden I/O that depends on which object is passed in. Integration tests calling `readEnv()` with no argument (for example delete-property.int.test.ts:11) do load the root `.env`. That happens not to matter only because the vitest `env` block sets every variable first.
  
  9. **apps/web/src/features/properties/property-filters.tsx:43-51**: a `prevApplied` state plus a set-state-during-render comparison keeps the draft in sync with the URL.
     - **Root change:** remount the form when the applied filter changes. In property-list.tsx:64, render `<PropertyFilters key={writeListParams({filter, direction}).toString()} …>` (or key on just the filter part) and delete the sync block and `sameFilter`.
     - **Cost:** it's easy to get wrong later (a new filter field has to be added to `sameFilter` too), and each change renders twice.
  
  10. **apps/web/e2e/properties.spec.ts:6-7**: `FAILING_ZIP` is redeclared with a "Matches FAILING_ZIP in weatherstack-stub.mjs" comment, because the stub module calls `listen()` at the top level and can't be imported for its constant.
      - **Root change:** move the stub's constants (and its server factory) into a module with no side effects that both files import. apps/api/test/weatherstack.ts:4 has the same "Matches … in vitest.config.ts" copy of the stub base URL.
      - **Cost:** small, but if one side drifts, the failure-path test passes for the wrong reason or times out.
  
  11. **Zip rule copied in five places**: create-property.service.ts:48, list-properties.service.ts:36, validate-property.ts:28, property-filters.tsx:59, list-search-params.ts:26. Three of those copies are in the web app.
      - **Root change:** for the web app, one exported `isZipCode` / `ZIP_MESSAGE` in the properties feature. The server rule stays the source of truth.
      - **Cost:** low, but a rule change touches five files. This is more a reuse issue than an altitude one, so it's a minor note.
  
  **Areas that look clean at this altitude:**
  - **Resolvers:** the results-to-GraphQL-union mapping and `WEATHER_MESSAGES` are presentation concerns and belong where they are. The invalid-filter error is decided in the service.
  - **Apollo type policies** (apps/web/src/apollo.ts): `merge: false` on `properties` and `merge: true` on id-less `Weather` are the right fixes at the mechanism level.
  - **Sonner:** `toast.dismiss()` sits in the central test setup (apps/web/src/test/setup.ts:12-14), not per test. That's the right place for a library-global store.
  - **Playwright webServer config:** the `exec` process-group fix and the IPv4 host are infrastructure fixes, applied once in config.
  - **Repository:** the P2002 race fallback and the `escapeLike` helper are at the right depth.
  - **Also clean:** the Weatherstack client, container injection, ESLint layering rules (verbose but deliberate), Claude hooks, CI, Dockerfile and compose files.
</agent-message>

  I found 16 simplifications I'm confident about, 10 in the app and 6 in tests and config. Nothing was edited. All paths are under ~/Projects/covertree-properties.
  
  **Web app (apps/web/src)**
  
  1. **features/properties/property-filters.tsx:41-51**: state that could be derived from props.
     - Now: the component keeps a copy of `applied` in `prevApplied`, compares it with `sameFilter` (lines 27-28), and calls `setDraft` and `setZipError` during render to stay in sync.
     - Simpler: in property-list.tsx:64, render `<PropertyFilters key={writeListParams({filter, direction: SortDirection.DESC}).toString()} applied={filter} … />`. A remount then resets both `draft` and `zipError`, so `prevApplied`, `sameFilter` and the block at lines 47-51 can go.
     - Cost: one extra state variable, a hand-written equality function that must be updated whenever a field is added, and the setState-during-render pattern that readers find hard to follow.
  
  2. **features/properties/property-list.tsx:66-112**: a four-level nested ternary picks one of five UI states (error, loading, filtered-empty, empty, list).
     - Simpler: move it into a `ListBody` component that uses early returns, the same way `PropertyDetails` (property-details.tsx:24-67) already does.
     - Cost: the conditions depend on their order and are hard to scan. `properties?.length === 0` is repeated, and `properties?.map` has to stay optional-chained even though `properties` is known to be defined by then.
  
  3. **property-list.tsx:66-80 and property-details.tsx:24-41**: the "Could not load … / Check that the API is running / Retry" Alert is copy-pasted, differing only in the title.
     - Simpler: a shared `<LoadError title onRetry />`.
     - Cost: about 15 duplicated lines of JSX, and a copy or styling change has to be made twice.
  
  4. **property-list.tsx:26-29 and property-details.tsx:15-18**: the same `Intl.DateTimeFormat('en-US', {dateStyle:'medium', timeStyle:'short'})` is defined twice.
     - Simpler: export one formatter from a shared module.
     - Cost: the two dates can drift apart in format.
  
  5. **`Object.values(USState)` defined three times**: create-property-form.tsx:19, property-filters.tsx:8, and as a Set in list-search-params.ts:13. The state `<NativeSelect>` option list is also repeated (create-property-form.tsx:112-117, property-filters.tsx:109-114).
     - Simpler: one `US_STATES` constant, and a `StateOptions` component that takes the placeholder label ("Select…" / "Any").
     - Cost: three constants and two option loops to keep in sync.
  
  6. **The zip rule `/^\d{5}$/` is written in three places on the web side** (validate-property.ts:28, property-filters.tsx:59, list-search-params.ts:26), plus twice in the API (create-property.service.ts:48, list-properties.service.ts:36).
     - Simpler: an `isZip` helper, or a `ZIP` constant, per app.
     - Cost: a change to the rule has to be made in five places.
  
  7. **features/properties/list-search-params.ts:24**: `...NO_FILTER` is spread and then all three of its fields are overwritten on the next lines.
     - Simpler: delete the spread. That also removes list-search-params' only runtime import of property-filters.tsx (the `FilterValues` import is type-only).
     - Cost: dead code that suggests there are defaults when there are none.
  
  8. **create-property-form.tsx:35 and property-filters.tsx:53**: the curried `update(field)(value)` is only ever called as `update('x')(e.target.value)`.
     - Simpler: `update(field, value)`, or `onChange={(e) => update('street', e.target.value)}`.
     - Cost: a closure is created per render for no reason, and the call sites are harder to read.
  
  9. **create-property-form.tsx:86-87, 97-98, 108-109, 129-130**: `aria-invalid={!!errors.x}` and `aria-describedby={errors.x ? 'x-error' : undefined}` are repeated on all four inputs, even though `Field` already knows the `id` and the `error`.
     - Simpler: have `Field` produce those props, for example as a render-prop or with `cloneElement`, or pass them in as a prop object.
     - Cost: eight repeated lines, and an id can easily be mistyped (the `-error` suffix is built in two places).
  
  10. **routes/home.tsx**: a wrapper whose only job is `return <PropertyList />`.
      - Simpler: `{ index: true, Component: PropertyList }` in router.tsx.
      - Cost: a file that does nothing.
  
  **API (apps/api/src)**
  
  11. **services/create-property.service.ts:10-15**: `CreatePropertyInput` repeats the repository's `Address` field for field.
      - Simpler: `export type CreatePropertyInput = Address;`
      - Cost: two identical shapes to keep in sync.
  
  12. **services/list-properties.service.ts:56**: `const normalized: PropertyFilter = parsed.data;` exists only to add a type annotation.
      - Simpler: pass `filter: parsed.data` inline. It is already assignable to `PropertyFilter`.
      - Cost: minor noise.
  
  Everything else in the API is clean: app, container, env, repository, resolvers (the switch over the result union is appropriate), the get/delete services, and the weatherstack client and schema.
  
  **Tests and config**
  
  13. **apps/api/test/app.test.ts:14-18**: builds its own `app.fetch(... POST JSON ...)` instead of using the existing `executeOperation` helper in test/graphql.ts.
      - Simpler: `const { body } = await executeOperation(app, '{ __type(name: "Property") { name } }')`.
      - Cost: a duplicated request builder.
  
  14. **List-row test factories are duplicated.** `property()` in property-list.test.tsx:17-34 and property-filters.test.tsx:11-26 build the same list-row shape with slightly different signatures.
      - Simpler: add a `listedProperty(overrides)` next to `detailedProperty` in src/test/properties.ts.
      - Cost: two fixtures that will drift apart when the query changes.
  
  15. **Test constants are written twice.** `TEST_ACCESS_KEY` / `WEATHERSTACK_URL` in test/weatherstack.ts:5-6 are literal copies of the `'test-key'` / `'http://weatherstack.test'` values in vitest.config.ts:11-12. The base URL is written a third time in create-property.int.test.ts:264. Also, `WEATHERSTACK_URL` is exported but only used inside its own file.
      - Simpler: import both constants into vitest.config.ts (it already imports `TEST_DATABASE_URL` this way) and stop exporting `WEATHERSTACK_URL`.
      - Cost: nothing enforces that the copies match, which only the comment at line 4 points out.
  
  16. **Smaller items:**
      - **Default test DB URL and `:5433/` guard duplicated**: apps/web/playwright.config.ts:15-20 repeats both from apps/api/test/test-database-url.ts and global-setup.int.ts:7. Import `TEST_DATABASE_URL` across packages, or accept the duplication knowingly.
      - **Pointless alias**: apps/api/test/global-setup.int.ts:6, `const url = TEST_DATABASE_URL;`. Use the constant directly.
      - **Unneeded spread**: apps/api/src/weatherstack/client.test.ts:11, `...(timeoutMs === undefined ? {} : { timeoutMs })`. The destructuring default already applies to `undefined` (and `exactOptionalPropertyTypes` is false), so just write `timeoutMs`.
      - **Dead export**: apps/web/e2e/weatherstack-stub.mjs:10, `export const FAILING_ZIP`. Nothing imports it; the spec redeclares it at e2e/properties.spec.ts:7 because importing the stub would start its server. Drop `export`.
      - **Restated default**: apps/web/vite.config.ts:11, `server: { port: 5173 }` is Vite's default. Delete it.
      - **Restated defaults in compose**: docker-compose.yml:42-43, `WEATHERSTACK_BASE_URL: http://api.weatherstack.com` and `PORT: 4000` repeat the zod defaults in env.ts:7,9. Delete them.
      - **CI env block**: .github/workflows/ci.yml:13-18. `TEST_DATABASE_URL` matches the code default. `WEATHERSTACK_BASE_URL` / `WEATHERSTACK_ACCESS_KEY` appear unused, because vitest `test.env` and the Playwright `webServer.env` set their own values. `VITE_GRAPHQL_URL` equals the fallback in main.tsx:10. Only `DATABASE_URL` (for `db:drift`) looks needed. This one I inferred from reading the configs; I did not run CI.
      - **Repeated heading/push logic**: scripts/lib/render.mjs has `if (lastRole !== 'assistant') blocks.push('#### 🤖 Claude')` twice (lines 181/185). Also, the two `prompts++` conditions at lines 232-247 could be a single `if` with `||`. Hoist the header check above the branch and merge the conditions.
  
  **Clean:** the .claude/hooks scripts (small, shared lib.mjs, no dead code), scripts/archive-session.mjs, scripts/check-codegen.mjs, scripts/lib/redact.mjs, the Dockerfile, nginx.conf, the eslint layering config, both codegen configs, apollo.ts, delete-property-button.tsx, validate-property.ts, and the api test helpers database.ts, msw.ts and weatherstack.ts (apart from item 15).

  Efficiency review of chore/ai-harness vs main. I only read code and edited nothing. Findings are ordered by impact.
  
  **Build, CI and Docker**
  
  1. **~/Projects/covertree-properties/Dockerfile:16-18** — `COPY . .` comes before `pnpm install --offline`.
     - Any change to a source file, doc or test invalidates the install layer. It then re-runs the link step and postinstall (`prisma generate` plus `graphql-codegen` in both apps).
     - The `api` and `web-build` stages both start `FROM deps`. So a web-only edit also rebuilds the API (`tsc`), and an API-only edit rebuilds the Vite bundle.
     - Cheaper: copy only the `package.json` files, `prisma/schema.prisma` and the codegen configs and schema, then install. After that, `COPY apps/api` and `COPY apps/web` into separate stages. Or install with `--ignore-scripts` and run generate after the source copy.
     - Cost: about 20–40 s on every local `docker compose up --build`, plus one needless cross-app rebuild each time.
  
  2. **~/Projects/covertree-properties/.github/workflows/ci.yml:90-96** — the `docker` job runs a plain `docker compose build` with no layer cache.
     - Every run redoes `apt-get`, `npm i -g pnpm`, `pnpm fetch`, both builds and the nginx stage.
     - Cheaper: `docker/setup-buildx-action` plus `docker/bake-action` or `build-push-action` with `cache-from/cache-to: type=gha`.
     - Cost: about 1–3 min per CI run.
  
  3. **ci.yml:80** — the `e2e` job runs `pnpm run build` before e2e, but nothing uses the output.
     - Playwright starts the API with `tsx src/server.ts` and the web app with the Vite dev server (`apps/web/playwright.config.ts:45,60`).
     - The build also repeats work other jobs already do: `web build` runs `tsc --noEmit` (the `typecheck` job does that), and both apps are built again in the `docker` job.
     - Cheaper: drop the step, or make e2e serve the built output (`vite preview` / `node dist/server.js`) so the build is actually tested.
     - Cost: about 30–60 s on the longest job's critical path.
  
  4. **ci.yml:81** — `playwright install --with-deps chromium` runs uncached on every run.
     - Cheaper: cache `~/.cache/ms-playwright` keyed on the Playwright version, and only run `install-deps` when the cache hits.
     - Cost: about 30–60 s per run.
  
  5. **~/Projects/covertree-properties/apps/api/package.json:18, apps/web/package.json:13** — postinstall runs `graphql-codegen` in both apps, even though the generated GraphQL types are committed.
     - All 5 CI jobs pay for this in the shared setup action. Local installs and the Docker install do too.
     - `scripts/check-codegen.mjs:8` then runs codegen a third time.
     - Cheaper: keep only `prisma generate` in postinstall, because the Prisma client is gitignored.
     - Cost: a few seconds per job, so about 10–20 s of CI minutes per run.
  
  6. **~/Projects/covertree-properties/apps/web/nginx.conf** — no `gzip on;` (or gzip_static), and gzip is off by default in `nginx:alpine`.
     - The JS and CSS bundle is served uncompressed.
     - Cheaper: `gzip on; gzip_types text/css application/javascript application/json image/svg+xml;`.
     - Cost: about 3–4x more bytes on every first load.
  
  7. **Dockerfile:20-26** — the `api` runtime image is the full workspace `node_modules`: web deps, Vite, Playwright's package, Radix and so on.
     - Cheaper: `pnpm deploy --filter api /out` (which keeps its dev deps, so the Prisma CLI is still there) and copy that into a slim stage.
     - Cost: probably several hundred MB of image size, plus the time to push and pull it.
  
  **Claude Code hooks (these run on every edit or stop)**
  
  8. **~/Projects/covertree-properties/.claude/hooks/format-lint.mjs:19-27** — calls `pnpm exec prettier` and then `pnpm exec eslint`.
     - Each `pnpm exec` pays pnpm's own startup (about 0.3–0.6 s) before the tool starts.
     - `hasBin()` already confirms `node_modules/.bin/<tool>` exists, so spawn that directly, as `playwright.config.ts` already does.
     - Cost: about 0.6–1.2 s on every Edit/Write.
  
  9. **~/Projects/covertree-properties/.claude/hooks/stop-check.mjs:33-41** — runs `typecheck` and then `test:unit` one after the other, across every package, whatever changed.
     - They are independent, so run them at the same time (spawn both, await both).
     - Cheaper still: pass only the packages touched by `changed` (`pnpm --filter api...`).
     - Adding `"incremental": true` (tsbuildinfo) to the tsconfigs would make repeat typechecks much faster.
     - Cost: roughly the shorter of the two runs (several seconds) on every Stop that has source changes. Typecheck time on repeat stops drops to a fraction.
  
  10. **~/Projects/covertree-properties/.claude/hooks/codegen.mjs** — a second Node process starts on every Edit/Write, only to exit straight away for anything that isn't `.graphql` or `schema.prisma`.
      - Cheaper: fold its extension check into `format-lint.mjs`, making it one hook process.
      - Cost: about 40–80 ms per edit. Small, but it's paid on every edit.
  
  **API**
  
  - **~/Projects/covertree-properties/apps/api/src/services/create-property.service.ts:79-99** — the check-then-insert looks redundant but is intentional: it skips the Weatherstack call for duplicates, and P2002 covers the race. Clean.
  - Repository, resolvers and startup are also clean. There are no N+1s, since `Weather` is a JSON column resolved in memory. Schema and SDL are read once at module load. The indexes match the queries.
  
  **Web / Apollo**
  
  11. **~/Projects/covertree-properties/apps/web/src/features/properties/create-property.mutation.ts:8-10** — on success the mutation selects only `property { id }`, then the app navigates to the detail page.
      - `PropertyQuery` (cache-first) therefore always makes a second round trip.
      - Cheaper: select the detail fields (a shared fragment with `property.query.ts`) in the mutation, so the detail page renders straight from the cache.
      - Cost: one request (DB read plus latency) saved on every create.
  
  12. **~/Projects/covertree-properties/apps/web/src/features/properties/property-list.tsx:43** — `fetchPolicy: 'cache-and-network'` refetches the whole list on every mount, including each back-navigation from a detail page.
      - Cheaper: keep cache-first and, in the create mutation's `update`, run `cache.evict({ fieldName: 'properties' })` followed by `cache.gc()`. Delete already evicts.
      - Cost: one full-list query (with the JSONB weather for every row) saved per list → detail → back trip. This is minor at the current data size.
  
  **Tests**
  
  13. **~/Projects/covertree-properties/apps/api/test/filter-properties.int.test.ts:28-35** — truncates and runs 5 separate `seedProperty` inserts before each of 6 tests, but only S3.8 changes data (it truncates by itself).
      - Cheaper: seed once in `beforeAll` with a single `createMany`, and let S3.8 reset around itself.
      - Cost: about 30 DB round trips per run. Small. The other integration files' per-test `TRUNCATE` is cheap and fine as is.
      - Timeout tests already use 50–100 ms timeouts, not the real 5 s. Clean.
  
  **Session archiving (runs detached, so only CPU matters)**
  
  14. **~/Projects/covertree-properties/scripts/lib/redact.mjs:50-52** plus **scripts/archive-session.mjs:65** — `redact()` rebuilds `homeRules()` on every call, and it is called once per JSONL line.
      - Each rebuild costs an `os.userInfo()` syscall and 2 fresh RegExps.
      - Cheaper: build the combined rule list once at module load, and redact the whole file in one call; no pattern crosses a newline.
      - `archive-session.mjs:89-91` also reads back every file it just wrote to scan for leaks. Scan the in-memory strings instead.
      - Cost: scales with transcript size (thousands of lines); low priority.
  
  **Clean areas:** docker-compose (tmpfs test DB, healthchecks), CI concurrency and cancel, the test global setup (runs `migrate deploy` once per run), web test render setup, and the Weatherstack client.
